clue.text: Danish king eventually supporting the necessary supporters

parts.note: if you are supporting a cause you are for it
both are old slang for money

explanation.surface: A Danish monarch who in time comes to back the people propping him up.
explanation.walkthrough: In Hamlet the Norwegian prince Fortinbras arrives at the end and takes the Danish throne, hence 'eventually'.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's Norwegian prince claims Denmark's crown in the final scene of Hamlet, once the royal family lies dead.

clue.text: Fruity bar, nothing else

explanation.surface: Order a fruity drink at the bar and nothing more.
explanation.walkthrough: Said at the end of a statement, the phrase means 'and that is all there is to it'.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying the phrase after a statement signals that there is no more to add, meaning that is the end of it.

clue.text: Bird to carry off home

parts.note: to rob is to steal, carrying goods away
being in means being at home

explanation.surface: A bird bearing something back to its nest.
explanation.definitionFit: The robin is a small red-breasted garden songbird.

clue.text: Chess piece in woollen ski pants is quirky idea

indicators.note: 'in ... is' says what is found inside the jumbled phrase, placing the idea within it
pants is British slang for rubbish, so the clothing words are a poor arrangement to be redone

parts.note: a whim is a sudden fanciful notion

explanation.surface: Someone thinks a chess piece wearing knitted ski trousers is a fun notion.
explanation.walkthrough: Chess is the Tim Rice musical, and this song from it was a UK number one for Elaine Paige and Barbara Dickson. 'Pants' looks like trousers but is slang for rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: This duet is a famous number from the musical Chess, so it is literally a piece from that show.

clue.text: Perhaps Chelsea will have drawn German team

parts.note: a Chelsea bun is a sticky currant bun
D for drawn, as in football league tables

explanation.surface: A football forecast: Chelsea will draw against a German side.
explanation.walkthrough: Chelsea looks like the London football club, but it is the bun.
explanation.definitionFit: Bund is German for a league or federation, a group banded together, as in Bundesliga.

clue.text: Predictably take a second glance around you?

indicators.note: around means the reading word encloses the short pronoun

parts.note: a perusal is a reading-over, here a quick look

explanation.surface: Of course you would look again at yourself.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means in the customary way, just as was expected, so things happening predictably.

clue.text: Country club tolerated

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for clubs in card games
as in 'I won't have it', to have is to put up with

explanation.surface: A country club that was merely put up with.
explanation.definitionFit: Chad is a landlocked nation in north-central Africa.

clue.text: House on very short section of US boundary

indicators.note: short means cut off at the end, so the last letter goes

parts.note: HO is the abbreviation for house
on top of something is over it

explanation.surface: A house sitting on a tiny stretch of the American border.
explanation.walkthrough: The dam spans the Colorado River on the state line between Nevada and Arizona, so it forms part of an internal boundary.
explanation.definitionFit: This huge concrete dam stands across the Colorado River where it marks the Nevada–Arizona state line.

clue.text: Process to stop kid talking

indicators.note: talking means the words are taken as spoken sounds

explanation.surface: A procedure for getting a child to stop chattering.
explanation.definitionFit: To digest information is to take it in and work through it, as the body processes food.

clue.text: Scrap metal 4 presumably

parts.note: the answer's first word acts as the anagram signal acting on the words that follow it in the answer

indicators.note: presumably signals a reverse clue: the answer itself is the instruction that would turn the words before it into part of the answer

explanation.surface: Scrap metal of some sort, with a cross-reference.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: read the answer as a clue, 'rough' as an anagram signal and AND TUMBLE as its result, and metal plus BUND is what you would roughen.
explanation.definitionFit: A scrap is a disorderly fight, and a rough-and-tumble is exactly that kind of untidy brawl.

clue.text: Tyre setting restriction applied, chasing finishers in final race

indicators.note: finishers are the closing letters, so only the ends of the following words count

parts.note: the last letter of each of these two words

explanation.surface: A motor-racing tale of tyre rules imposed after the end of the last race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tyre' is not the rubber on a car but the ancient port city, so 'Tyre setting' is the country it stands in. 'Chasing' puts the restriction after the finishers.
explanation.definitionFit: The Phoenician city of Tyre lies on the coast of this Middle Eastern state, so the state is where it is set.

clue.text: Trident component? Left-over parts causing delay

definitions.note: verb phrase: to prolong is to cause things to drag on

indicators.note: the outer word parts, splitting open so something sits between its two halves

parts.note: O is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for an over

explanation.surface: Spare bits of a trident holding up the job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left-over' reads as one word but splits into two abbreviations; in cricket an over is a set of six balls.
explanation.definitionFit: To prolong something is to extend its duration, making it last longer and so holding up its end.

clue.text: Crime starts to excite when you're tough

indicators.note: starts are opening letters, so only the first of each following word is used

parts.note: the initials of these three words

explanation.surface: Breaking the law thrills you when you are a hard case.
explanation.definitionFit: Sinewy meat is stringy and hard to chew, and a sinewy person is wiry and strong.

clue.text: Sex? For rather than against going …

indicators.note: the word meaning 'against' inside the first word is swapped for the one meaning 'for'

parts.note: sexual congress, a formal word for intercourse

explanation.surface: A question about sex, voting in favour rather than opposing, with the thought running on into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: CON at the start of CONGRESS is replaced by PRO. The ellipsis carries the sentence on into 15 across.
explanation.definitionFit: Progress is forward movement, and 'going' as a noun likewise means headway made on a journey.

clue.text: Hunks — blokes entertaining English girl

indicators.note: to entertain a guest is to hold them in your home, so one word takes another inside

explanation.surface: Muscular men chatting up an English girl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hunks' suggests attractive men, but an old meaning of hunks, singular, is a miser.
explanation.definitionFit: Hunks is an archaic word for a stingy, miserly person, which is exactly what a skinflint is.

clue.text: … hammer and tongs in the casual version of it

indicators.note: to hammer something is to batter it out of shape, so the words after it are knocked into a new order

parts.note: as written; it also reads as a link, but its letters are needed

explanation.surface: Carrying on from 13 across: going at it hammer and tongs in a no-strings fling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hammer and tongs' looks like a fixed phrase, but 'hammer' is the anagram signal and 'and tongs in the' is the fodder. 'It' is sex, from 13 across.
explanation.definitionFit: A brief sexual encounter with no continuing relationship is the casual form of sex, here called 'it'.

clue.text: Community workers side with morphing monsters

parts.note: the European Community, now the European Union

indicators.note: morphing means changing shape, so the word next to it is reshaped

explanation.surface: Local labourers line up alongside shape-shifting creatures.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth these are the Furies, avenging female spirits often depicted as monstrous.

clue.text: Being shown old news about South American Indians

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the news letters go round the rest

parts.note: read as N's, two N's for new
the Cree are a Native American people

explanation.surface: Stale reports about South American tribes being broadcast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'South American Indians' reads as one group but splits: S, then the North American Cree.
explanation.definitionFit: Something on-screen is currently being displayed on a television or monitor, so it is being shown.

clue.text: Old country wine gets Madonna tipsy

parts.note: a sweet wine made from muscat grapes

indicators.note: a tipsy person is unsteady and muddled, so the singer's name is jumbled

explanation.surface: A vintage from some country gets the pop star Madonna drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old country wine' looks like a description of a rustic drink, but the definition ends at 'country'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sultanate of Muscat and Oman was the name of today's Oman until 1970, so it is a former state.

clue.text: Enemies of US love British gangsters

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, shaped like O

explanation.surface: America's foes are fond of British crooks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'US' looks like the United States but is just the pronoun.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mob is a collective name for organised crime, especially the Mafia and its members.

clue.text: Mess around with women in clean clothes? Yes, in a way

definitions.text: clean clothes? Yes, in a way

indicators.note: the mess word goes around the rest, enclosing it

parts.note: to make a hash of something is to mess it up

explanation.surface: Fooling about with women, then a question about laundering garments.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a question and answer: can you clean clothes this way? Yes, it is one method.
explanation.definitionFit: To handwash garments is to launder them by hand in a basin, one way of getting them clean.

clue.text: Old Irish Bill assumes it's backward country

indicators.note: to assume is to take on, so the police force takes the next word inside it

parts.note: the Royal Ulster Constabulary, Northern Ireland's former police; the Old Bill is slang for police

indicators.note: backward means the short word that precedes it is read from right to left

explanation.surface: An old Irish draft law takes on a backward country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like a parliamentary bill, but 'the Old Bill' is British slang for the police; the RUC was replaced in 2001.
explanation.definitionFit: Rustic describes things of the countryside, so it works as the adjective 'country', as in country cottage.

clue.text: Your health history?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a drink raised in someone's honour
second meaning: finished, done for, as in 'you're history'

explanation.walkthrough: 'Your health' is the words spoken when raising a glass.
explanation.definitionFit: Raising a glass while saying 'your health' is a tribute drink, and someone who is doomed is informally said to be finished.

clue.text: It's immature and wrong, dad admits

indicators.note: to admit is to let in, so the father word holds the other inside

parts.note: as in 'what's up?', something is amiss

explanation.surface: Father confesses something is childish and mistaken.
explanation.definitionFit: A pupa is an insect at the stage between larva and adult, so it has not yet matured.

clue.text: Old woman injecting drug to numb bone marrow

indicators.note: injecting puts something inside, so the old woman takes the rest within her

parts.note: to dull pain is to numb it

explanation.surface: Mum gives herself a shot of anaesthetic to numb a bone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bone marrow' sounds medical alongside the injection, but it is simply the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Medulla is the anatomical term for the inner core of an organ or bone, including the marrow.

clue.text: In naughty game, rub the hump

indicators.note: something naughty misbehaves, so these letters will not stay in order

explanation.surface: In some saucy game, players rub a hump.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang, to have the hump is to be sulky and offended.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking umbrage means feeling offended, the same sulky resentment as having the hump.

clue.text: Soprano comes in to bribe detective

indicators.note: comes in to means enters, so the letter sits inside the next word

parts.note: to buy someone is to bribe them

explanation.surface: An opera singer turns up to pay off a police officer.
explanation.walkthrough: A busy is old British slang, especially in Liverpool, for a policeman or detective.
explanation.definitionFit: British underworld slang uses this word for a plain-clothes police officer or detective.

clue.text: A Renault with 100mph acceleration power

parts.note: the Megane is a Renault model
doing a ton is driving at a hundred miles an hour

explanation.surface: A car advert boasting of a Renault's pace and pull.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Acceleration power' sounds like car marketing, but it is physics: force is mass times acceleration.
explanation.definitionFit: A meganewton is a million newtons, a unit of force, the quantity that produces acceleration in a mass.
